newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike threat raises health care worries.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike threat raises health care worries.

text.p: A strike at United Parcel Service of America Inc. could pose a threat to the delivery of drugs and medical supplies to hospitals and eventually could affect critically ill patients, drug companies said Friday.
Industry experts said a walkout by some 200,000 Teamsters union members at UPS likely would slow shipments of vital medical supplies, including drugs and surgical equipment.

"It's a major concern for us because it affects how we are going to get our medications to the people who need them, particularly critically ill patients," Amy Magan, a spokesman for pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly and Co., said.
Lilly relies on UPS for a significant portion of its product deliveries, Magan said, although it does maintain relationships with other carriers.
"We will do whatever we have to, use every other carrier we can, to get the drugs where they need to go," Magan said.
But she also said the company was concerned that other carriers won't be able to handle the additional load that Lilly and other major product shippers would require.

"UPS ships more than all the other carriers combined. There simply are not enough other carriers to pick up the slack," said Kathy Luhn, a spokeswoman with the National Industrial Transportation League, a Virginia-based trade association.
"The pharmaceutical companies would be among the first to be affected," Luhn added.

The healthcare industry, like most other businesses, relies increasingly on just-in-time delivery systems that help keep on-site inventories low. While that's good for the bottom line, it creates vulnerability to shipping disruptions, especially one as potentially huge as a UPS work stoppage.

"It's hard to gauge how big an effect it will have, but we're assuming it will cause some problems for our industry," said Jeff Trewhitt, a spokesman for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, a Washington-based trade group.
"I'm sure our members use UPS to some extent to ship lab results and equipment," Trewhitt said.
The mobility of the nation's blood supply, however, apparently is not at risk.
The American Red Cross relies on UPS rival Federal Express Corp. to handle express deliveries of blood around the country, Don Kirchoffner, a Red Cross spokesman, said.
"The blood supply won't be affected by a strike," Kirchoffner said. "No area will face a shortage because we couldn't move the blood."
UPS and representatives of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters were to resume last-ditch talks at 1 p.m. EDT while workers stayed on the job.
